current: The portion ends with Israelite men sinning with Moabite women at Baal Peor; the zealot Pinchas kills a flagrant offender and stops a plague.
problem: Pinchas kills two people, the Israelite man and the Midianite woman; 'a flagrant offender' leaves out the woman and makes it sound like one killing.
evidence: Numbers 25:8: 'stabbed both of them, the Israelite man and the woman, through the belly. Then the plague against the Israelites was checked.' https://www.sefaria.org/Numbers.25.8
fix: The portion ends with Israelite men sinning with Moabite women at Baal Peor; the zealot Pinchas kills an Israelite man and a Midianite woman, and the plague stops.

current: This is the Torah's one full narrative from outside Israel's perspective: Balak, king of Moab, watches Israel's victories with terror — 'they will lick up everything around us like an ox licking up the grass of the field' — and recruits the most effective prophet-for-hire in the ancient Near East, Balaam son of Beor from Pethor in Mesopotamia, to curse Israel.
problem: Two superlatives with no source: 'the Torah's one full narrative from outside Israel's perspective' and 'the most effective prophet-for-hire in the ancient Near East'. Also the 'lick up' line is spoken by Moab to the elders of Midian (22:4), not quoted from Balak.
evidence: Numbers 22:2-5: 'Balak son of Zippor saw all that Israel had done to the Amorites... Moab dreaded the Israelites, and Moab said to the elders of Midian, "Now this horde will lick clean all that is about us as an ox licks up the grass of the field." ... sent messengers to Balaam son of Beor in Pethor, which is by the Euphrates'; Deuteronomy 23:5: 'Balaam son of Beor, from Pethor of Aram-naharaim'. https://www.sefaria.org/Numbers.22.2-5 ; https://www.sefaria.org/Deuteronomy.23.5
fix: Balak, king of Moab, sees what Israel did to the Amorites, and Moab is filled with dread: 'this horde will lick clean all that is about us as an ox licks up the grass of the field.' Balak sends for Balaam son of Beor, from Pethor by the Euphrates in Aram-naharaim, to curse Israel.

current: His final oracle includes the famous line: 'How goodly are your tents, O Jacob, your dwelling places, Israel' (Mah tovu). He prophesies a star rising from Jacob and a scepter from Israel. Furious, Balak dismisses him.
problem: 'How goodly are your tents' (24:5) is in Balaam's third oracle, not his final one. Balak's angry dismissal (24:10-11) comes after the third oracle, and only then does Balaam give his last oracle with the star and scepter (24:15-17). The order is reversed.
evidence: Numbers 24:5 'How fair are your tents, O Jacob'; 24:10-11 'Enraged at Balaam, Balak... "you have blessed them these three times! Back with you at once to your own place!"'; 24:14,17 'let me inform you of what this people will do... A star rises from Jacob, A scepter comes forth from Israel'. https://www.sefaria.org/Numbers.24.10-17
fix: His third oracle includes the famous line: 'How goodly are your tents, O Jacob, your dwelling places, Israel' (Mah tovu). Furious, Balak tells him to go home, but before leaving Balaam gives a last oracle that foresees a star rising from Jacob and a scepter from Israel.

current: Moses's nephew Pinchas impales an Israelite man and Midianite woman caught in flagrant public transgression — and the plague stops.
problem: Pinchas is the son of Eleazar son of Aaron, so he is Moses's great-nephew, not his nephew. The Talmud has him call Moses 'brother of the father of my father'.
evidence: Numbers 25:7 'Phinehas, son of Eleazar son of Aaron the priest' https://www.sefaria.org/Numbers.25.7 ; Sanhedrin 82a: 'He said to Moses: Brother of the father of my father, as Moses was the brother of his grandfather Aaron' https://www.sefaria.org/Sanhedrin.82a
fix: Moses's great-nephew Pinchas, grandson of Aaron, drives a spear through an Israelite man and a Midianite woman caught in flagrant public transgression, and the plague stops.

current: Balaam is the only named non-Israelite prophet in the Torah who is presented as a genuine prophet of YHWH — not an idolater but someone who actually receives divine communication.
problem: 'Only' is unsourced, and 'not an idolater' goes against the text: Balaam used omens before (24:1), Joshua calls him an augur, and Numbers 31:16 blames the Peor sin on his advice. The paragraph itself later calls him 'a pagan prophet'.
evidence: Numbers 24:1 'did not, as on previous occasions, go in search of omens' https://www.sefaria.org/Numbers.24.1 ; Joshua 13:22 'Balaam son of Beor, the augur' https://www.sefaria.org/Joshua.13.22 ; Numbers 31:16 'at the bidding of Balaam, induced the Israelites to trespass against GOD in the matter of Peor' https://www.sefaria.org/Numbers.31.16 ; Numbers 22:38 'I can utter only the word that God puts into my mouth.' https://www.sefaria.org/Numbers.22.38
fix: Balaam is a non-Israelite whom God speaks to in the Torah, and he says he can utter only the word God puts in his mouth, though he had used omens before and Joshua 13:22 calls him an augur.

current: He also appears in an extraordinary archaeological find: the Deir Alla Inscription, discovered in 1967 in Jordan and dating to around 800 BCE, contains a lengthy prophetic text about 'Balaam son of Beor, a seer of the gods' — providing independent, non-biblical attestation that Balaam was a real figure known in the ancient Near East.
problem: Find year (1967), place (Jordan) and date (within the 880-770 BCE range) check out. But the inscription shows that a tradition about a seer named Balaam son of Beor was known in the region; it does not show that he was a real person, and its story differs from Numbers. Also, 'lengthy' oversells a text reconstructed from broken plaster fragments.
evidence: Wikipedia, Deir Alla inscription: 'discovered during a 1967 excavation in Deir Alla, Jordan'; dated '880-770 BC'; describes Balaam as 'a seer of the gods' with an account that differs from Numbers. Search summary of the same article: 'a series of ink on plaster fragments'. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deir_Alla_inscription
fix: He also appears in an archaeological find: the Deir Alla inscription, ink on plaster fragments found in 1967 in Jordan and dated to roughly 880-770 BCE, tells of 'Balaam son of Beor, a seer of the gods', which shows that stories about a seer with this name were told in the region outside the Bible.

current: The Mah Tovu prayer — 'How goodly are your tents, O Jacob' — opens the morning synagogue service to this day, so Jewish prayer begins every day with words spoken by a pagan prophet hired to curse Israel.
problem: Only the first line of Mah Tovu is Balaam's; the rest is from Psalms. It is a custom said on entering the synagogue at the start of morning prayers, not a universal start of 'Jewish prayer every day'. 'Pagan prophet' also clashes with the paragraph's own opening sentence ('not an idolater').
evidence: Wikipedia, Ma Tovu: 'recited by Jews at the beginning of the morning prayers when one would theoretically have just entered the synagogue'; describes the first line as coming from Balaam. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ma_Tovu
fix: The Mah Tovu prayer, which opens with Balaam's words 'How goodly are your tents, O Jacob', is said by many Jews at the start of morning prayers, on entering the synagogue.

current: The Mishnah (Avot 5:19) contrasts 'the students of Abraham' with 'the students of Balaam,' characterizing Balaam as the archetype of a person with good eyes but bad character.
problem: The Mishnah says the opposite about the eye: a 'good eye' is a mark of Abraham's students, and an 'evil eye' is a mark of Balaam's.
evidence: Pirkei Avot 5:19: 'A good eye, a humble spirit and a moderate appetite he is of the disciples of Abraham... An evil eye, a haughty spirit and a limitless appetite he is of the disciples of Balaam' (Heb. עַיִן רָעָה... מִתַּלְמִידָיו שֶׁל בִּלְעָם). https://www.sefaria.org/Pirkei_Avot.5.19
fix: The Mishnah (Avot 5:19) contrasts 'the disciples of Abraham' with 'the disciples of Balaam': Abraham's have a good eye, a humble spirit and a moderate appetite, while Balaam's have an evil eye, a haughty spirit and a limitless appetite.

current: Pinchas's act — killing the transgressing couple — is one of the Torah's most controversial moments, celebrated as zealotry that stopped a plague but also generating enormous rabbinic discomfort about vigilante violence; the Talmud notes that had Pinchas asked a rabbinic authority whether to do it, he would have been told not to.
problem: The Talmud states a general rule, that a court does not instruct someone who comes to ask whether to strike such an offender. It does not say Pinchas would have been told not to; in the same passage Pinchas does ask Moses, who answers 'Let the one who reads the letter be the agent'.
evidence: Sanhedrin 82a: 'Rav Hisda says: Concerning one who comes to consult with the court... the court does not instruct him that it is permitted to kill the transgressor'; and 'He said to Moses: ... did you not teach me... zealots strike him? Moses said to him: Let the one who reads the letter be the agent to fulfill its contents.' https://www.sefaria.org/Sanhedrin.82a
fix: Pinchas's act, killing the couple, is one of the Torah's most controversial moments: it is praised for stopping a plague, yet the Talmud (Sanhedrin 82a) rules that if someone comes to ask the court whether to strike such an offender, the court does not tell him to do it.

current: The Amarna Letters from Canaan mention Baal worship as standard practice in the region.
problem: The Amarna letters do mention the storm god (read Addu or Ba'lu) and use 'my Baal' as a title for the Egyptian king, but they are diplomatic letters, not a description of Baal worship as 'standard practice'.
evidence: Jewish Virtual Library, Baal Worship (Encyclopaedia Judaica): 'In the El-Amarna letters Canaanite clients addressed the Egyptian king as "My Baal, my Addu."' and 'the logogram for the weather-god is conventionally read Addu, but... sometimes to be read Ba'lu'. https://jewishvirtuallibrary.org/baal-worship-jewish-virtual-library
fix: The Amarna letters, sent by rulers in Canaan to the king of Egypt, refer to the weather god Baal (also called Addu), and some even address the Egyptian king as 'my Baal'.

current: Pagan prophets-for-hire — specialists who could access divine power for practical purposes — are attested in Mesopotamian texts, where professionals could be engaged to curse enemies using incantation techniques.
problem: The comparison with Mesopotamian specialists is a scholarly suggestion, and a disputed one: the best-known parallel, the baru, was a diviner who read omens, not someone hired to curse enemies. Stated here as settled fact.
evidence: TheTorah.com, Ethan Schwartz, 'Balaam from Divinerville': Daiches argued 'Balaam fits the profile of the type of Mesopotamian diviner known as a baru', but critics object that this 'unjustifiably conflates... divination... and magic... Whereas the baru was an expert in the former, Balak hires Balaam to do the latter.' https://www.thetorah.com/article/balaam-from-divinerville
fix: Some scholars compare Balaam to the Mesopotamian baru, a trained diviner who read omens, though others point out that the baru read the gods' will, while Balak hires Balaam to curse.

current: God validates Pinchas's act with a covenant of peace and everlasting priesthood — his descendants will hold the High Priesthood in perpetuity.
problem: The verse promises Pinchas and his descendants 'a covenant of priesthood for all time' (kehunat olam); it does not say 'High Priesthood'. Going beyond the verse.
evidence: Numbers 25:13: 'It shall be for him and his descendants after him a pact of priesthood for all time' (Heb. בְּרִית כְּהֻנַּת עוֹלָם). https://www.sefaria.org/Numbers.25.13
fix: God rewards Pinchas's act with a covenant of peace and a covenant of priesthood for all time, for him and his descendants after him.

current: A second census is then taken of the new generation (the first was in Bamidbar, at the start of the wilderness journey): the first generation who left Egypt has almost entirely died out, exactly as decreed after the spy episode, with only Caleb and Joshua surviving among the scouts.
problem: The verse says Caleb and Joshua are the only survivors of everyone counted at Sinai, not just the only surviving scouts. The narrower wording misses the point of 26:64-65.
evidence: Numbers 26:64-65: 'Among these there was not one of those enrolled by Moses and Aaron the priest... in the wilderness of Sinai... Not one of them survived, except Caleb son of Jephunneh and Joshua son of Nun.' https://www.sefaria.org/Numbers.26.64-65
fix: A second census is then taken of the new generation (the first was in Bamidbar, at the start of the wilderness journey): as God decreed after the spy episode, not one of the men counted at Sinai is left except Caleb and Joshua.

current: The daughters of Zelophechad — Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah — are named four times in the Torah (here, in the next chapter, in Joshua 17, and in 1 Chronicles 7), an unusual distinction that the rabbis read as an indication of their extraordinary wisdom and righteousness.
problem: Joshua and Chronicles are not in the Torah. The Torah names them three times (Num 26:33, 27:1, 36:11), and Joshua 17:3 names them a fourth time; 1 Chronicles 7:15 only says Zelophehad 'had daughters'. 'The next chapter' is also off: 26:33 and 27:1 are both in Pinchas, and the third listing is in Masei (36:11). The Talmud calls them wise and righteous, but not because of how many times they are named.
evidence: Numbers 26:33, 27:1, 36:11 and Joshua 17:3 list the five names; 1 Chronicles 7:15: 'and Zelophehad had daughters' (no names). https://www.sefaria.org/Numbers.26.33 ; https://www.sefaria.org/Numbers.36.11 ; https://www.sefaria.org/Joshua.17.3 ; https://www.sefaria.org/I_Chronicles.7.15 ; Bava Batra 119b: 'The daughters of Zelophehad are wise, they are interpreters of verses, and they are righteous.' https://www.sefaria.org/Bava_Batra.119b
fix: The daughters of Zelophechad, Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah, are named three times in the Torah (Numbers 26:33, 27:1 and 36:11) and again in Joshua 17:3, and the Talmud (Bava Batra 119b) calls them wise, skilled interpreters of Scripture, and righteous.

current: Their case is cited in the Talmud (Bava Batra 119b) as proof that they were wiser than Moses himself in reading the legal situation: 'The daughters of Zelophechad said something that Moses's comprehension did not reach.'
problem: Bava Batra 119b does not contain this quote or say they were wiser than Moses. It says they were wise, skilled interpreters and righteous, and that they spoke at the right moment, while Moses was teaching the law of levirate marriage.
evidence: Bava Batra 119b: 'The Sages taught: The daughters of Zelophehad are wise, they are interpreters of verses, and they are righteous. ... That they are wise can be seen from the fact that they spoke in accordance with the moment...' (no statement comparing them to Moses's understanding). https://www.sefaria.org/Bava_Batra.119b
fix: The Talmud (Bava Batra 119b) praises them: 'The daughters of Zelophehad are wise, they are interpreters of verses, and they are righteous.'

current: The laying of hands (semikhah) by Moses on Joshua is the foundational act of rabbinic ordination: every ordained rabbi in history received authority through an unbroken chain of semikhah going back — in theory — to this moment of Moses laying hands on Joshua, creating a continuous thread of authorized leadership across three millennia.
problem: The classical chain of semikhah stopped in late antiquity (between 360 and 425 CE). Modern rabbinic ordination is a different, later institution and does not claim an unbroken chain from Moses. So 'every ordained rabbi in history' and 'continuous thread... across three millennia' are wrong.
evidence: Wikipedia, Semikhah: 'This form of semikha ceased between 360 and 425 CE'; modern ordination is 'generally through an institution, a yeshiva or specialized kollel' and differs from the original, which required 'a court of three judges'. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semikhah ; Numbers 27:23 'He laid his hands upon him and commissioned him' https://www.sefaria.org/Numbers.27.23
fix: Moses laying his hands on Joshua (semikhah) became the model for the ancient rabbinic ordination of the same name; that original chain of ordination ended in late antiquity, and today's rabbinic ordination is a later form that keeps the name.

current: The Elephantine papyri (5th century BCE Jewish community in Egypt) show Jewish women owning property and engaging in legal transactions, suggesting the inheritance laws here had real practical application in ancient Jewish communities.
problem: The papyri do show women receiving and holding property (by gift and dowry), but nothing in them ties this to the law of Numbers 27; scholars note the Elephantine Jews seem not to have known a written Torah. The conclusion does not follow.
evidence: Wikipedia, Elephantine papyri and ostraca: 'Ananiah transferred ownership of an apartment... to his wife, Tamut'; the house given 'to their daughter, Yehoishema, as payment on her dowry'; the Jews there 'seem to have had no knowledge of a written Torah or the narratives described therein'. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elephantine_papyri_and_ostraca
fix: The Elephantine papyri, from a Jewish community in Egypt in the 5th century BCE, show Jewish women receiving houses as gifts and dowries and taking part in legal transactions.

current: A woman's vow, however, can be annulled by her father while she lives in his house, or by her husband when she marries — a reflection of the patriarchal social structure of the ancient world that later legal tradition would significantly qualify.
problem: The first half matches the verses. The added claim that later legal tradition 'would significantly qualify' this is given no source and is not explained; it is editorial commentary presented as fact.
evidence: Numbers 30:4-6: 'If a woman makes a vow... while still in her father's household by reason of her youth... But if her father restrains her on the day he finds out, none of her vows... shall stand'; 30:14 'Every vow and every sworn obligation of self-denial may be upheld by her husband or annulled by her husband.' https://www.sefaria.org/Numbers.30.3-6
fix: A woman's vow, however, can be annulled by her father while she is young and still in his household, or by her husband.

current: The war spoils are divided between fighters, community, and the Levites with meticulous mathematical precision; warriors who have killed must undergo purification, and metal vessels captured must be purified through fire or water.
problem: The split leaves out the priest: one in five hundred of the fighters' half goes to Eleazar the priest, and one in fifty of the community's half goes to the Levites. Metal that can withstand fire goes through fire and must also be cleansed with water of lustration; things that cannot withstand fire go through water.
evidence: Numbers 31:27-30: 'divide the booty equally between the combatants... and the rest of the community... one item in five hundred... given to Eleazar the priest... one in every fifty... give them to the Levites'; 31:23 'any article that can withstand fire... pass through fire... except that they must be cleansed with water of lustration; and anything that cannot withstand fire you must pass through water.' https://www.sefaria.org/Numbers.31.19-23 ; https://www.sefaria.org/Numbers.31.27-30
fix: The spoils are split in half between the fighters and the rest of the community, with a set share of each half going to Eleazar the priest and to the Levites; everyone who has killed or touched a corpse must be purified, and captured metal goes through fire and water.

current: Moses accepts this conditional agreement and formalizes it with Joshua and Eleazar as witnesses.
problem: The verse says Moses gave instructions about the agreement to Eleazar, Joshua and the tribal family heads, who are to carry it out (give them Gilead if they fight); it does not call them witnesses.
evidence: Numbers 32:28-29: 'Then Moses gave instructions concerning them to Eleazar the priest, Joshua son of Nun, and the family heads of the Israelite tribes... you shall give them the land of Gilead as a holding.' https://www.sefaria.org/Numbers.32.28-29
fix: Moses accepts this conditional agreement and gives Eleazar, Joshua and the tribal heads instructions to carry it out.

current: This makes it the only battle in the entire Torah described as having no Israelite deaths, which the rabbis found so remarkable they read it as a miracle equivalent to the splitting of the sea.
problem: No source found for the rabbis comparing this to the splitting of the sea. The Talmud (Shabbat 64a) reads 'not one of us is missing' a different way: none of the soldiers had sinned as at Shittim. 'Only battle in the entire Torah' is also unsourced.
evidence: Shabbat 64a: 'Moses said to Israel: Perhaps you have returned to your original sinful behavior, when you sinned with the daughters of Moab and Midian at Shittim? They said to him: "Not one man of us is missing" (Numbers 31:49), we remain as wholesome in deed as we were.' https://www.sefaria.org/Shabbat.64a ; Numbers 31:49 https://www.sefaria.org/Numbers.31.49
fix: The Talmud (Shabbat 64a) also reads the words as a moral claim: none of the soldiers had sinned as the people did at Shittim.

current: The tribes of Reuben and Gad settling east of the Jordan created the longest-running political division in Israelite history: the Transjordanian tribes were always somewhat separate from the main Israelite community west of the river, a division that contributed to the northern kingdom's eventual independence and the lasting tension between different Israelite communities.
problem: No source for 'longest-running political division' or for the claim that the east-west split helped cause the northern kingdom's break-away; 1 Kings 12 gives Rehoboam's heavy yoke as the cause. Tension over the eastern tribes is attested in Joshua 22.
evidence: 1 Kings 12:4 'Your father made our yoke heavy. Now lighten the harsh labor...' https://www.sefaria.org/I_Kings.12.4 ; Joshua 22:10-12: the Reubenites, Gadites and half-tribe of Manasseh 'built an altar there by the Jordan'... 'the whole community of the Israelites assembled at Shiloh to make war on them.' https://www.sefaria.org/Joshua.22.10-12
fix: The settlement of Reuben and Gad east of the Jordan later caused friction: in Joshua 22 the western tribes almost go to war over an altar the eastern tribes build by the Jordan.

current: The laws of vows in this portion became the basis for Kol Nidre — the most famous Jewish prayer, chanted on the eve of Yom Kippur, which annuls vows made rashly or under duress between the individual and God for the coming year. Kol Nidre is technically a legal formula for annulment of vows, rooted directly in the laws stated here about the binding nature of vows and the possibility of annulment.
problem: Kol Nidre is not a prayer but a legal declaration, and 'most famous' is an unsourced superlative. Its words annul personal vows generally, not specifically 'rash or under duress' ones. Its direct source is the Talmud's rule on declaring future vows void (Nedarim 23b), not the annulment laws of Numbers 30, which are about a father or husband. 'For the coming year' is the Ashkenazi wording after Rabbeinu Tam; the older wording covered the past year.
evidence: Wikipedia, Kol Nidre: 'Kol Nidrei is not a prayer, it makes no requests and is not addressed to God, rather, it is a juristic declaration'; Rabbeinu Tam 'changed the original phrase "from the last Day of Atonement until this one" to "from this Day of Atonement until the next"'. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kol_Nidre ; Nedarim 23b: 'one who desires that his vows not be upheld for the entire year should stand up on Rosh HaShana and say: Any vow that I take in the future should be void.' https://www.sefaria.org/Nedarim.23b
fix: This portion's laws of vows stand behind Kol Nidre, the declaration said on the eve of Yom Kippur that cancels personal vows (in the common Ashkenazi wording, those of the coming year). Its direct basis is the Talmud's rule (Nedarim 23b) that a person may declare in advance that his future vows will be void.

current: The Gad and Reuben compromise — 'we will not return to our homes until every Israelite has taken possession of their inheritance' — became a model in rabbinic literature for the principle that all of Israel is responsible for one another (kol Yisrael arevim zeh lazeh).
problem: The quote matches Numbers 32:18, but no source was found tying this verse to 'kol Yisrael arevim'. The Talmud derives that principle from Leviticus 26:37, 'they shall stumble one upon another'.
evidence: Shevuot 39a: '"And they shall stumble one upon another" (Leviticus 26:37)... which teaches that the entire Jewish people are considered guarantors for one another.' https://www.sefaria.org/Shevuot.39a ; Numbers 32:18 'We will not return to our homes until the other Israelites are in possession of their portion.' https://www.sefaria.org/Numbers.32.18
fix: The Gad and Reuben pledge, 'We will not return to our homes until the other Israelites are in possession of their portion' (32:18), shows the tribes taking responsibility for one another.

current: The Transjordanian territories of Gilead, Bashan, and the plains of Moab that Reuben and Gad requested were fertile uplands with excellent grazing — the archaeological record confirms significant pastoral activity in these regions throughout the Iron Age.
problem: Reuben and Gad asked for 'the lands of Jazer and Gilead'; Bashan (Og's kingdom) went to them together with half of Manasseh, and the plains of Moab were not requested. The archaeological claim has no source.
evidence: Numbers 32:1 'Noting that the lands of Jazer and Gilead were a region suitable for cattle'; 32:33 'to the Gadites, the Reubenites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh... the kingdom of Sihon... and the kingdom of King Og of Bashan'. https://www.sefaria.org/Numbers.32.1 ; https://www.sefaria.org/Numbers.32.33-38
fix: Reuben and Gad asked for the lands of Jazer and Gilead, east of the Jordan, because the region was good for cattle; Moses gave them, with half of Manasseh, the former kingdoms of Sihon and of Og of Bashan.

current: The cities they are described as rebuilding — Dibon, Ataroth, Aroer, Heshbon, and others — are all identifiable archaeological sites in modern Jordan, some of which have been extensively excavated.
problem: 'All identifiable' is too strong: the list in 32:34-38 also includes towns such as Sibmah whose location is uncertain, with rival proposed sites. Dibon (Dhiban) is securely identified and excavated.
evidence: Numbers 32:34-38 lists Dibon, Ataroth, Aroer, Atroth-shophan, Jazer, Jogbehah, Beth-nimrah, Beth-haran, Heshbon, Elealeh, Kiriathaim, Nebo, Baal-meon, Sibmah https://www.sefaria.org/Numbers.32.33-38 ; Easton's via BibleStudyTools: Sibmah 'has been identified with the ruin of Sumieh' https://www.biblestudytools.com/dictionary/sibmah/ , while other dictionaries place it at Khirbet al-Qibsh (search results); Wikipedia, Dhiban: 'The Mesha Stele linked the tell at Dhiban with the biblical Divon'; excavations from 1950 on. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhiban,_Jordan
fix: The cities they are described as rebuilding include Dibon, Ataroth, Aroer and Heshbon, east of the Jordan in modern Jordan; some, like Dibon (modern Dhiban), are known and excavated, while others on the list are still debated.

current: The laws of war spoils — dividing captured goods between warriors, community, and priests with specified percentages — reflect a systematized approach to plunder that had parallels in other ancient Near Eastern armies.
problem: No source given or found for the ancient Near Eastern parallels. The division also includes the Levites, not only priests.
evidence: Numbers 31:27-30: half to combatants, half to the community; one in five hundred of the fighters' half to Eleazar the priest; one in fifty of the community's half to the Levites. https://www.sefaria.org/Numbers.31.27-30
fix: The laws of war spoils divide the captured goods in half between the warriors and the community, with fixed shares from each half for the priest and the Levites.

current: The borders of the Promised Land are defined and the tribes assigned portions.
problem: No tribe is given its portion in Masei. The land is to be divided later by lot, and the portion only names the men who will divide it (Eleazar, Joshua and a chieftain from each tribe).
evidence: Numbers 34:13 'This is the land you are to receive by lot as your hereditary portion... to the nine and a half tribes'; 34:17-18 'These are the names of the men through whom the land shall be apportioned for you: Eleazar the priest and Joshua son of Nun. You shall also take a chieftain from each tribe'. https://www.sefaria.org/Numbers.34.13-18
fix: The borders of the Promised Land are defined, and leaders are named to divide it among the tribes by lot.

current: First, Moses records all forty-two stopping points of the journey from Egypt: Ramesses, Succoth, Etham, Pi-HaHiroth, the sea, the wilderness of Shur, Marah, Elim, the wilderness of Sin, and so on, camp by camp — a sparse travel diary of forty years compressed into a single chapter that reads like both a geographic record and a meditation on how far they have come.
problem: Numbers 33 does not name the wilderness of Shur here: after the sea they go three days 'in the wilderness of Etham' to Marah (Shur is the name in Exodus 15:22). The list also skips a camp: between Elim and the wilderness of Sin they camp by the Sea of Reeds (33:10).
evidence: Numbers 33:8-11: 'passed through the sea into the wilderness; and they made a three-days' journey in the wilderness of Etham and encamped at Marah. They set out from Marah and came to Elim... They set out from Elim and encamped by the Sea of Reeds. They set out from the Sea of Reeds and encamped in the wilderness of Sin.' https://www.sefaria.org/Numbers.33.5-12 ; Rashi on 33:1: 'there are here only forty-two stages' https://www.sefaria.org/Rashi_on_Numbers.33.1
fix: First, Moses records all forty-two stages of the journey from Egypt: Rameses, Succoth, Etham, Pi-hahiroth, through the sea and three days in the wilderness of Etham to Marah, then Elim, the Sea of Reeds, the wilderness of Sin, and so on, camp by camp — a sparse travel diary of forty years compressed into a single chapter.

current: The connection between the killer's release and the High Priest's death is explained by later commentators as the High Priest's spiritual power of atonement being transferred at death — his death atones for the nation's inadvertent sins, including accidental homicide.
problem: The Talmud says the High Priest's death atones for the killer's sin; nothing found about a 'power of atonement being transferred' or about atoning for 'the nation's inadvertent sins'. Rashi gives other reasons: the High Priest should have prayed that no such accident happen in his days.
evidence: Makkot 11b: 'It is the death of the High Priest that atones for his sin' https://www.sefaria.org/Makkot.11b ; Rashi on Numbers 35:25: 'Because the High Priest should have prayed that this misfortune might never happen in Israel in his days (cf. Makkot 11a)'. https://www.sefaria.org/Rashi_on_Numbers.35.25

current: The forty-two stopping points of the wilderness journey are mapped by the rabbis as corresponding to forty-two stages of spiritual development in a person's life.
problem: This teaching is not from 'the rabbis' in general; it is a Hasidic teaching of the Baal Shem Tov, reported by his grandson in Degel Machaneh Ephraim (the jewishTradition field already attributes it correctly).
evidence: Degel Machaneh Ephraim, Masei: 'שמעתי בשם אא"ז זללה"ה כי כל המסעות היו מ"ב והם אצל כל אדם מיום הולדו עד שובו אל עולמו' (I heard in the name of my grandfather that all the journeys were 42, and they occur in every person from the day of his birth until he returns to his world). https://www.sefaria.org/Degel_Machaneh_Ephraim,_Masei
fix: The Baal Shem Tov, as his grandson reports in Degel Machaneh Ephraim, taught that the forty-two journeys happen in every person's life, from birth until death.

current: The Talmud (Makkot 10a-13b) devotes extensive analysis to defining 'accidental' versus 'intentional' killing, and the cities of refuge system was seen as a precursor to the rabbinic system of careful distinction between categories of homicide.
problem: The Talmud's chapter on exile to cities of refuge is Makkot chapter 2, which runs from 7a to 13a (chapter 3 begins on 13a). The 'precursor' claim has no source.
evidence: Makkot 7a (start of chapter 2): 'These are the people who are exiled: Anyone who kills a person unintentionally' https://www.sefaria.org/Makkot.7a ; Makkot 13a: 'MISHNA: After enumerating in tractate Sanhedrin those liable to be executed and in the previous chapter those liable to be exiled...' https://www.sefaria.org/Makkot.13a
fix: The Talmud devotes the second chapter of tractate Makkot (7a-13a) to deciding which kinds of unintentional killing send a person into exile in a city of refuge.

current: The land boundaries defined in this portion — from the Wadi of Egypt (Nahal Besor) in the south to Lebo-Hamath in the north, from the Mediterranean to the Jordan — correspond to the boundaries of the Egyptian province of Canaan during the New Kingdom, and to the territorial extent of David's and Solomon's kingdoms at their height. This 'ideal Israel' boundary is never fully achieved in the biblical narrative but becomes the territorial vision that motivates prophetic and royal claims throughout the monarchic period.
problem: Three problems. The Wadi of Egypt is usually identified with Wadi el-Arish; Nahal Besor is one scholar's proposal (Na'aman). The link to the New Kingdom Egyptian province is a hypothesis (Mazar), and other scholars date the borders to Pharaoh Necho's conquests in 609 BCE. And the passage contradicts itself: it says the borders match Solomon's kingdom, then says they are never achieved in the biblical narrative; the Bible does describe Solomon's Israel as reaching 'from Lebo-hamath to the Wadi of Egypt' (1 Kings 8:65).
evidence: Wikipedia, Brook of Egypt: 'A number of scholars have identified it with Wadi al-Arish'; 'Nadav Na'aman believes that the landform referenced in the Bible is the Besor Stream'. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brook_of_Egypt ; Yigal Levin, TheTorah.com: 'Mazar's hypothesis was that these boundaries reflect those of the thirteenth-century Egyptian province of Canaan'; 'I believe that the establishment of the northern border at Lebo-hamath... had more to do with the conquest of the area by Necho king of Egypt in 609 BCE'. https://www.thetorah.com/article/the-geopolitical-context-behind-the-boundaries-in-numbers-34 ; 1 Kings 8:65 'from Lebo-hamath to the Wadi of Egypt' https://www.sefaria.org/I_Kings.8.65
fix: The borders defined in this portion run from the Wadi of Egypt (usually identified with Wadi el-Arish, though some scholars propose Nahal Besor) in the south to Lebo-hamath in the north, and from the Mediterranean to the Jordan. Some scholars, following Benjamin Mazar, think they reflect the Egyptian province of Canaan in the 13th century BCE; others link them to the Egyptian conquests of Pharaoh Necho in 609 BCE. The Bible later describes Solomon's Israel as reaching 'from Lebo-hamath to the Wadi of Egypt' (1 Kings 8:65).

current: The forty-two wilderness stations, while some are obscure, include identifiable locations like Kadesh Barnea, the Arnon River, and the plains of Moab near Jericho.
problem: The Arnon River is not one of the stations in Numbers 33 (it appears in the journey story of Numbers 21:13). The list also calls the site 'the wilderness of Zin, that is, Kadesh', not Kadesh Barnea.
evidence: Numbers 33:36 'encamped in the wilderness of Zin, that is, Kadesh'; 33:44-49 lists Iye-abarim, Dibon-gad, Almon-diblathaim, the hills of Abarim, and 'the steppes of Moab, at the Jordan near Jericho' (no Arnon). https://www.sefaria.org/Numbers.33.36 ; https://www.sefaria.org/Numbers.33.44-49
fix: The forty-two wilderness stations, while some are obscure, include Kadesh in the wilderness of Zin, Dibon-gad, and the steppes of Moab by the Jordan near Jericho.
